meta.title: Who really said "We are what we think. All that we are arises with our thoughts. With our thoughts we make the world"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The Buddha never said this in these words. It’s Thomas Byrom’s loose 1976 verse translation of the Dhammapada’s opening — a rendering scholars call a mistranslation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We are what we think. All that we are arises with our thoughts. With our thoughts we make the world'?
meta.ogDescription: Not the Buddha’s words. This is Thomas Byrom’s much-criticized 1976 verse translation of the Dhammapada’s opening lines.

answer.label: Not the Buddha’s words — Thomas Byrom’s 1976 rendering
answer.sourceLine: These exact words open Thomas Byrom’s 1976 verse translation of the Dhammapada, an ancient Buddhist anthology traditionally ascribed to the Buddha. But the wording is Byrom’s own loose rendering: the Pali original (Manopubbaṅgamā dhammā…) says mind precedes and shapes our mental states — it never mentions ‘thoughts’ or making ‘the world.’ Pali scholars treat Byrom’s version as a poetic mistranslation, so this is not a documented saying of the Buddha.

source.excerpt: We are what we think. All that we are arises with our thoughts. With our thoughts we make the world.
trail: Buddhist teacher Bodhipaksa (Fake Buddha Quotes) traces the wording to Thomas Byrom’s translation ↗ and argues it “Hinduizes” a text that in Pali mentions neither ‘thoughts’ nor ‘the world.’
Quote Investigator ↗ quotes the passage as Byrom’s Dhammapada rendering and finds recent, unsupported reassignments to Emerson (c. 2009) and Lao Tzu (c. 2010).
Tricycle: The Buddhist Review ↗ published the same critique, recommending Fronsdal’s more faithful translation over Byrom’s.
Byrom (d. 1991), an Oxford- and Harvard-trained literary scholar and Advaita Vedanta practitioner, also translated the Hindu Ashtavakra Gita as The Heart of Awareness.
source.excerptNote: Byrom’s rendering continues into the familiar “Speak or act with an impure mind / And trouble will follow you” couplet. More literal translations read very differently — Buddharakkhita: “Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are all mind-wrought,” and Gil Fronsdal: “All experience is preceded by mind, / Led by mind, / Made by mind.” Neither speaks of making ‘the world.’

A 1976 translation by an identifiable translator is in copyright in the United States; the rights rest with Byrom’s estate and his publishers.

author.name: Thomas Byrom
author.heading: Who actually wrote this line
author.metaLine: d. 1991 · English literary scholar & verse translator of the Dhammapada
author.bio: Thomas Byrom was an English literary scholar educated at Balliol College, Oxford, and Harvard, where he taught history and literature. A practitioner of Advaita Vedanta who later lived and taught at Kashi Ashram in Florida, he also rendered the Hindu Ashtavakra Gita into English as The Heart of Awareness. His 1976 verse Dhammapada (with a foreword by Ram Dass) is loved for its lyricism but faulted by Pali scholars for reading nondual Hindu ideas into a Buddhist text.

misattribution.heading: How this became a ‘Buddha’ quote
misattribution.intro: The line is real — it opens a genuine translation of a genuine Buddhist scripture — but the leap from “the Dhammapada’s opening” to “the Buddha said, word for word” papers over a translator’s heavy hand.

items.why: The Dhammapada is traditionally ascribed to the Buddha, but this English phrasing is Thomas Byrom’s. Bodhipaksa notes the Pali says mind precedes and shapes our mental states and “mentions neither ‘thoughts’ nor ‘the world,’” so “with our thoughts we make the world” is Byrom’s interpolation (Fake Buddha Quotes ↗).
Quote Investigator finds the Emerson tag “apparently occurred in recent times” — e.g. a 2009 book — with no substantive backing (QI ↗).
Likewise recent and unsupported; the earliest instance QI documents is a 2010 Goodreads entry (QI ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: It is the opening of the Dhammapada as rendered by Thomas Byrom in 1976 — a lyrical but much-criticized paraphrase, not a faithful transcript of the Buddha’s words (Tricycle ↗).

context.heading: Why the wording matters
lead: The dispute here isn’t whether a wise text exists — it does. It’s that Byrom’s poetry quietly converts a psychological teaching into a metaphysical one. The Pali says the quality of your mind shapes whether your experience is suffering or joy; Byrom’s “with our thoughts we make the world” sounds instead like the mind literally manufactures external reality — a claim closer to Advaita Vedanta than to early Buddhism.

That shift is why the line thrives in law-of-attraction and self-help circles while Buddhist scholars wince at it. The idea traces to the Buddhist tradition; the memorable slogan traces to one translator in 1976.
context.pull: A psychological teaching became a metaphysical slogan — in translation.
